reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, the gene for the type 1 tumour necrosis factor receptor
Febrile attacks are notably longer than in most other periodic fever syndromes, often lasting one to three weeks
Migratory myalgia overlying a spreading erythematous rash is characteristic and reflects underlying fasciitis
Periorbital oedema with conjunctivitis and periorbital pain is a distinctive clue
Serositis causing abdominal or chest pain and arthralgia commonly accompany attacks
Acute-phase reactants are markedly elevated during flares and may remain elevated between them
Secondary AA amyloidosis is an important long-term risk, particularly with certain high-penetrance mutations
IL-1 inhibition is generally effective; TNF-directed therapy has variable and sometimes paradoxical responses
reference.pathophysiology: Mutations in TNFRSF1A impair normal shedding and folding of the type 1 TNF receptor, causing intracellular retention and misfolding of the receptor with activation of stress and inflammatory signalling pathways. Enhanced production of interleukin-1 and other proinflammatory mediators drives prolonged systemic and localised inflammation of skin, muscle fascia, serosal surfaces, and joints.
additionalDifferentials: Familial Mediterranean fever and other hereditary periodic fevers
Cellulitis or infective myositis (given the rash and myalgia)
Recurrent or chronic serositis of other causes
additionalInvestigations: Acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR, serum amyloid A) during and between attacks
Full blood count showing leukocytosis during flares
Urinalysis for proteinuria to screen for amyloidosis
Imaging or biopsy of affected muscle/fascia when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Persistent proteinuria indicating secondary AA amyloidosis with risk of renal failure
Prolonged unremitting fever prompting exclusion of infection or malignancy
High-penetrance mutation genotype associated with greater amyloidosis risk
Severe serositis mimicking a surgical or cardiac emergency
reference.prognosis: Attacks tend to recur over many years; with effective IL-1 targeted therapy inflammation is well controlled and amyloidosis risk reduced, but poorly controlled disease, especially with high-penetrance genotypes, carries a meaningful risk of amyloid nephropathy.
pitfalls: Confusing the migratory rash and myalgia with recurrent cellulitis and giving repeated antibiotics
Assuming attacks are too long to represent a periodic fever syndrome
Overlooking amyloidosis screening in long-standing disease
Expecting a uniform response to TNF inhibitors, which can be unpredictable
management: Interleukin-1-targeted therapy with anakinra or canakinumab as the mainstay to control recurrent attacks and dampen chronic inflammation
Corticosteroids to terminate or attenuate acute febrile attacks, with NSAIDs for fever, myalgia, and serositis
Reserve etanercept for where IL-1 inhibition is unavailable, and avoid monoclonal anti-TNF agents such as infliximab which may exacerbate disease
Serial monitoring of C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A, with urinalysis for proteinuria to detect AA amyloidosis
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
Multidisciplinary rheumatology-led care with nephrology input should amyloid nephropathy arise
Escalate biologic therapy for high-penetrance genotypes or breakthrough inflammation to reduce amyloidosis risk
